_comment: Toriano's villagers (stage 3). Schedules use the city's nav spots; 'when' switches schedules by flag: on Christmas Eve everyone is in the cathedral square from five.

npcs.name: Signor Augusto Viganò
npcs.title: Portinaio of Number 14

lines: Did you hear the bells? Forty years in the chorus and I never sang under a sound like that. Buon Natale, {name}.
Ah, {name}! The stairs are mopped, the post is sorted, and the courtyard smells of Signora Elvira's minestrone. All is well at number 14.
This way, this way! The gate with the iron lilies. You can't miss it. Everyone misses it.
{name}? The Geometra from Monteforchetta? Welcome to Toriano! I'm Augusto, the portinaio of number 14. Your new home. Well. Your new address.

sleepy: Mmm… la donna è mobile… zzz…

topics.label: You sang at the opera?
lines: Thirty-one years in the chorus of the Teatro Civico. Third from the left, always. In the photos you can see my elbow.
Maestro Gino was the prompter even then. He whispered the words to me in 1974 and I've never forgotten them. I've forgotten the opera, but not the words.

topics.label: Is it always this foggy?
lines: Only from October to March. And sometimes in April. And on a Tuesday in July once, but nobody believes me.
If you get lost, follow the tram rails. Every rail in Toriano leads back to the cathedral, or to the depot, which is nearly as holy.

topics.label: What's in the lodge?
lines: The post, the keys, the meter readings, and the lost property of half the neighbourhood. People drop everything in the fog. Umbrellas, gloves, their dignity.
I keep it all. One day somebody will come back for a single brown glove, and I will be ready.

gifts.line: A slice of panettone, from my own tin. Don't tell the Ragioniere. He thinks the tin is a building expense.
The plans of the bookshelf in my lodge. Every good portinaio needs somewhere to hide the post.

lines: Signor proprietario! Your share of the stair-lighting is due on the first. I say it with affection. And a receipt.
Sala. Ragioniere Sala. Administrator of number 14. Every repair needs a residents' meeting, a vote and three quotes. I have the forms.

topics.label: What are the building's rules?
lines: Rule one: no washing on the balcony railings. Rule two: Signora Elvira ignores rule one. Rule three: see rule two.
The rest are in the regulations of 1953, amended 1961, 1978 and twice in 1994 after the business with the goat.

topics.label: Time is money?
lines: Time is money, money is time, and a residents' meeting is a great deal of both.
I bill in quarter hours. This conversation has cost the building four hundred lire.

gifts.line: A refund. The building overcharged you for the stair lighting. It happens once every eleven years. Enjoy it.
The plans of my filing cabinet. Fireproof, fog-proof and, if you lose the key, Geometra-proof.

npcs.name: Architetto Ludovica Annoni
npcs.title: Head of the Cathedral Works

lines: Six hundred and twelve years, and the Angel has never looked so pleased with herself. Nearly finished, {name}. 2130 at the latest.
Up on the roof, everything slows down. Even the pigeons. That is where the cathedral does its thinking.
You must be the Geometra. Good. The Cathedral Works has been waiting for you. Not long. Only since 1387.
There's no hurry. There is never any hurry here. Everyone else in Toriano is late for something. We are early for the year 2130.

sleepy: The thirty-fourth pinnacle… is leaning… zzz…

topics.label: What is the Cathedral Works?
lines: The office that builds the cathedral. We started in 1387 and we are nearly finished. We've been nearly finished since 1813.
Marble comes up the canal by barge, the masons carve it in the yard, and every year something falls off and we start again. It's a living building. It sheds.

topics.label: How many statues are there?
lines: Three thousand four hundred and two. I know every one by name. The one over the south door with the startled face is Ambrogio the Lesser. He saw the bill.
And on the top spire, the Golden Angel. She used to shine over the square every Christmas Eve. The floodlight broke in 1989. Nobody had the plans.

topics.label: Why is everyone in a hurry?
lines: Because they measure their lives in minutes. I measure mine in centuries. It's very restful.
Ask the Ragioniere what time it is. Then ask me. You'll get very different answers, and mine will be approximately the fifteenth century.

gifts.line: Offcuts from the yard. Candoglia marble, the pink vein. Build something that lasts. Or at least something that lasts until Tuesday.
The plans of a statue from the archive. 1624. Nobody remembers who it was meant to be, so it can be anyone. It looks a bit like you.

npcs.name: Ambrogio Colombo
npcs.title: Tram Driver ("il Tranvee")

lines: My last run, {name}. Thirty years, never late in any fog. Carlotta rang her bell all the way round the square. I think she was crying. Trams do that.
Ding ding! Ambrogio Colombo, driver of the number 1 since 1969. They call me il Tranvee. My tram is Carlotta. Be nice to her, she's sensitive about her brakes.

sleepy: Next stop… zzz… Duomo… mind the… zzz…

topics.label: Who's Carlotta?
lines: My tram! Number 1503, built 1928. Wooden seats, brass handles, and a bell that can stop a bus at fifty metres.
She's been round the loop more times than the moon's been round the Earth. I did the sums once on a long red light.

topics.label: How do you drive in this fog?
lines: By ear. Every crossing has its own sound. The bakery hums, the bank clicks, and the cathedral square sounds like pigeons arguing.
Thirty years, never late. Once early, in 1983. I've never forgiven myself.

topics.label: Are you retiring?
lines: On Christmas Eve. My last run, round the square at midnight. After that, it's the young ones with their automatic doors.
Carlotta will go on without me. I've told her it's not her fault.

gifts.line: Some coils of the old overhead wire. Copper, the good stuff. They're replacing it with something that hums in a key I don't like.
Thirty years of tips from passengers. Well, a few of them. Buy yourself a hot chocolate. With cream. Ambrogio's orders.

lines: Twelve regulars, all here by nine, all dry. That's your bridge. I've put your name on the slate. Nobody's name goes on the slate.
…Good evening. Or morning. In here it's always about half past seven. What can I get you? Take your time. Everybody else in this city is in a hurry. Not in here.

topics.label: Who are your regulars?
lines: Twelve of them. Same twelve since 1962. The last new regular was in 1979, and he still sits by the door in case it doesn't work out.
I know all their secrets. I don't tell them. That's the job. That, and the coffee.

topics.label: What's in the canal?
lines: Bicycles, mostly. People ride home from here in the fog and the Naviglio takes its share.
Fish me some out and I'll hang them on the wall. A bar needs a theme. Mine is 'bicycles the canal gave back'.

gifts.line: Two hot chocolates, coffee and cream, the way they make it in Turin. On the house. Don't tell the twelve.
The plans of my bar counter. Walnut, 1962. It's heard more confessions than the cathedral.

npcs.name: Chiara Pozzi
npcs.title: Seamstress in the Galleria

lines: They stop at the window now, {name}! A lady from Paris asked if I ship. I said yes. I've no idea how. I'll learn.
Ciao! Mind the pins. This is my workshop, the smallest in the Galleria. Two metres by two. The rent is enormous. Per square centimetre, it's the most expensive room in Europe.

sleepy: Hem… hem… zzz… a dart there… zzz…

topics.label: You're a designer?
lines: I will be. Pozzi, a label. Padded jackets in colours nobody's brave enough for, and scarves big enough to get lost in, which in this fog is a feature.
For now I take in hems. Lots of hems. Everybody in Toriano is in a hurry, so they all tread on their trousers.

topics.label: What's the Galleria like?
lines: Glass roof, mosaic floor, and a bull in the mosaic that you spin on with your heel for luck. Don't tell Annoni. She says it's three hundred years of wear on one tile.
At Christmas they hang lights under the glass. You'll see.

gifts.line: Offcuts! Velvet, wool, a bit of tartan. Make something cosy. Or something outrageous. Ideally both.
My rug pattern. I wove the first one from forty old ties. You can tell which ones were from weddings.

lines: (whispering) The whole score. Every page. Tonight I'll whisper it to the tenors and they'll sing it as if they'd always known it. They never do.
(whispering) Good evening. Forgive me, I only whisper. Forty years in the prompter's box under the stage. If I spoke up, I'd ruin the second act.

topics.label: What does a prompter do?
lines: (whispering) I sit in a little box under the front of the stage and whisper the words to the singers when they forget them. Which is always.
(whispering) I know every opera by heart. All of them. I've never seen one. I've only ever seen ankles.

topics.label: You know Augusto?
lines: (whispering) Augusto Viganò! Third from the left. A lovely baritone and the worst memory in the chorus. I whispered him through thirty-one years of Christmas concerts.
(whispering) He still hums the overture when he mops the stairs. I can hear it from here. In my head.

gifts.line: (whispering) Two tickets' worth for the gallery. Sell them, or come and listen. Bring a cushion. The gallery seats are from 1891.
(whispering) The design of the old opera poster. Hang it somewhere quiet. Posters prefer quiet.

npcs.name: Ottavio Re
npcs.title: Keeper of the Parco dei Platani

lines: The ducks have moved in. They've already argued about the bedrooms. That's how you know it's a home.
Morning. Ottavio. I keep the park. Same loop every morning for twenty-five years, fog or no fog. I could walk it blindfold. In this fog, I do.

topics.label: What are these trees?
lines: Plane trees. They shed their bark like old wallpaper and their leaves like the city sheds its tourists, all at once in November.
They need pruning every winter or they grow into the tram wires. Ambrogio and I have an arrangement. I prune, he doesn't swear.

topics.label: And the ducks?
lines: Forty-two of them, give or take. The old duck house sank in the flood of '94. They've been sleeping on the bench ever since, and the bench is not happy.

gifts.line: Prunings from the plane trees. Good dry wood. Take it before the ducks start building with it.
The plans for the park hedges. Plant them in rows. Hedges like rows. Ducks like hedges. Everybody wins.

npcs.name: Gennaro Russo
npcs.title: Chestnut Seller at the Castle Gate

lines: Look at her! A counter, a roof, a lamp! The chestnuts taste better under a roof. It's science. Neapolitan science.
Caldarroste! Hot chestnuts! Ah, a new face. Gennaro Russo, from Campania, roasting chestnuts at this gate every winter since 1986. Warm your hands, they're free. The chestnuts aren't.

topics.label: What's the weather tomorrow?
lines: Fog in the morning, fog at lunch, and in the evening, surprise: fog. My knee is never wrong. The weatherman on the TV is always wrong. He has two good knees.
But I'll tell you a secret. One night before Christmas, it's going to snow. My knee is very excited about it.

topics.label: Your cart's seen better days.
lines: My cart is older than my marriage and has fewer working parts. Every winter a wheel falls off. Every spring my wife says 'Gennaro, a new cart.' Every winter, the wheel.

gifts.line: Three cones, extra hot. Give them to someone you like. Or eat them all yourself. I won't tell.
Take this. You keep buying my chestnuts. A man should get something back from his best customer.

lines: Now they see me! Every car, every bus, a cyclist from Bergamo who was very surprised. Rocco Spreafico, visible at last!
*FWEEEET!* Halt! Ah, a pedestrian. Carry on. Vigile Rocco Spreafico, traffic police. They call us 'Ghisa', for the old helmets. Mine is white. Spotless. Look at it.

topics.label: Who are you directing?
lines: The traffic! There's always traffic. Sometimes I can't see it, in the fog, but I know it's out there. Somewhere. Turning left illegally.
On a foggy morning in 1995 I directed traffic for two hours before I found out I was in the park. The ducks were very well behaved.

topics.label: Nice helmet.
lines: Thank you. White, so they see me. Except in the fog, where white is exactly the problem. Nobody thought this through in 1890.

gifts.line: Confiscated hubcaps. I'm not supposed to give these away. You didn't see me. Nobody ever does.
The plans of a proper road sign. Point it wherever you like. Then point it the other way. Toriano won't notice.
My old helmet. The white one, from before they gave us the new ones. In the fog, people will stop when they see you. Mostly.

npcs.name: Vale Meroni
npcs.title: Junior Reporter, La Sera di Toriano

lines: THE FRONT PAGE, {name}! My name, your name, the Angel in colour! They've given me a desk with a window. The window faces a wall. It's a start!
Vale Meroni, La Sera di Toriano! Can I quote you? You're the new Geometra! Say something about the city! Anything! Not 'foggy', everyone says foggy.

topics.label: How do I get in the paper?
lines: Do things! Help people, build things, fix things. I write it up, the editor measures it with a ruler, and you get column inches. More inches, bigger story.
Ten inches gets you a notice by the crossword. A hundred and twenty gets the front page. I've never had the front page. I've had the weather, twice.

topics.label: What's the big story in Toriano?
lines: The Golden Angel! She hasn't shone on Christmas Eve since 1989. If she lights up again, that's the front page. Christmas Day. Colour photo.
Annoni says it'll happen 'in due course'. Her due course is about four hundred years. I need it by December.

gifts.line: My fee for the quote you gave me. You said 'busy'. The editor loved it. Busy! So true!
The plans of a newsroom desk. Ink-proof, coffee-proof, deadline-proof. Mostly.

lines: My professor came round to see it. He said 'derivative but promising'. That's the nicest thing he's ever said! He said it about your pergola, but still!
Oh hey, neighbour! Simone. Architecture, fourth year, eighth attempt at the exam. Sorry about the music. It's Ninth Wave. They're Belgian. You'll get used to them.

topics.label: What are you building?
lines: Models! Cardboard, glue, a lot of glue. My flat is forty per cent cardboard by volume. The Ragioniere says it's a fire risk. I say it's a portfolio.
My exam model is a pergola. Four pillars, a roof, two benches. Very simple. Very pure. The professor says it doesn't stand up. It's cardboard. Of course it doesn't stand up.

topics.label: And Signora Elvira?
lines: She brings me soup and complains about the music. Then she taps her foot to it. I've seen her. She knows all the words now.

gifts.line: Offcuts from my models. Balsa, mostly. It's not strong but it's very light. Like my arguments, the professor says.
My pillar drawings! Proper ones, to scale. A Geometra should have them. A student shouldn't, apparently. I photocopied them from the library.

npcs.name: Signora Elvira Marelli
npcs.title: Neighbour at the End of the Balcony

lines: A real tree in the courtyard, with lights! Like before the war. Well. Like after the war. Before the war we had a goat. Long story.
Ah, the new one in number 3. Welcome, welcome. Elvira Marelli. I'm the end of the balcony. That's my washing over your window. You'll learn to love it.

topics.label: What was the courtyard like?
lines: Before the war? Children, chickens, a fig tree, and a Christmas tree every year that the whole building decorated with whatever it had. One year it was spoons.
Now it's bicycles and the Ragioniere's notices. The bicycles are nicer.

topics.label: The toilet's down the balcony?
lines: Shared, at the end, past my door. Everyone in the building has met everyone in the building in the queue for it. That's how I met my husband. 1958.
He was in there forty minutes. I married him anyway.

gifts.line: Some flowers from my balcony and a bit of lace. Put them in your flat. A flat without flowers is just a box with a radiator.
How to make a proper window box. Write it down. No, I'll write it down. You young people only remember things on your computers.
